subject: Whether to approve a ~$41k/month active-active, two-region architecture project next quarter to meet the availability SLA in the largest customer contract (Halvorsen Logistics, Schedule C)
decisionObjective: Decide whether to approve, reject, defer or re-scope the multi-region active-active project. The test is whether it is the most cost-effective way to cut the real risk of breaching the contracted SLA (99.95% monthly over a 30-day month, with service credits) and of losing the customer, compared with cheaper fixes aimed at the failure modes the incident log actually shows.

criteria.name: Fit between the proposed fix and observed failure causes
criteria.rationale: The project only pays off if it removes the downtime that actually happens. The incident log attributes most customer-facing minutes to bad deploys, certificate expiry and a third-party API, and records zero region-wide outages. Active-active across regions does not prevent any of these, and a deploy that reaches both regions can take both down.

criteria.name: Correct SLA target and downtime budget arithmetic
criteria.rationale: The VP's premise ties 99.99% to about 52 minutes a month. Over a 30-day month 99.99% allows about 4.3 minutes; 52.6 minutes is the yearly figure. The contract requires 99.95%, which allows about 21.6 minutes a month. Which target applies, and how big its budget really is, determines whether the project is needed at all.

criteria.name: Contractual exposure: credits, breach history and termination risk
criteria.rationale: The dollar value of avoided breaches sets the upper bound on what is worth spending. Credits are 10% of monthly fees per full 0.1% below target. A breach of 0.1% is about 43 minutes, so the past misses (for example 38 and 22 minutes) may have triggered no credit or a small one. The true size of the risk depends on monthly fees and on any termination or chronic-breach clauses.

criteria.name: Total cost of ownership versus alternatives
criteria.rationale: The cost is about $492k a year in infrastructure plus 2 engineers for 2 quarters. It should be compared with targeted measures such as safer deploys (canary, progressive rollout, automated rollback, migration discipline), certificate automation and third-party fallbacks, and with warm-standby or pilot-light DR as a cheaper hedge against region loss.

criteria.name: Implementation and data-consistency risk
criteria.rationale: The ledger DB needs multi-region writes, and its consistency model and RPO/RTO are still TBD. Active-active writes on a financial ledger bring correctness risk (split-brain, conflicting writes) and new failure modes. During the transition this can lower availability rather than raise it.

criteria.name: Strategic and other-customer value of regional resilience
criteria.rationale: A region-loss event has low probability but high impact. Other customers, sales requirements or regulatory and DR expectations could justify some regional redundancy even if this contract's SLA does not. That value should be weighed separately from the SLA case.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: 99.99% availability 'still gives us around 52 minutes of downtime a month'
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Recompute: 0.0001 x 30 days x 1440 min = 4.32 min per month. 52.56 min is the yearly allowance. Also compute 99.95%: 21.6 min per month.
Compare with contract clause C.1, which specifies 99.95%. Check whether any other contract or business requirement demands 99.99%.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: Region failure is the biggest availability risk
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Group the incident log by cause and sum minutes. The log records 0 region-wide outages and a majority of minutes from bad deploys. Add the provider's historical regional-outage frequency.
Review the platform team estimate. It covers infrastructure only. Add 2 engineers x 2 quarters, ongoing operational overhead and any ledger DB licensing or replication costs to get the full TCO.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: Active-active multi-region would materially improve measured availability against this SLA
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Map each incident to whether a second active region would have prevented it. Consider whether global deploys, shared config or cross-region data replication would spread the same failures to both regions.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The incident log is complete and its customer-facing minutes match how the contract measures availability
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Check the log against monitoring data and the contract's definition of availability and maintenance exclusions. Confirm that no incidents are missing and that the minutes are counted per 30-day month.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The project can be delivered next quarter
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: The estimate states 2 quarters of engineering and lists the ledger consistency model and RPO/RTO as TBD. Confirm the timeline with the platform team.

evidenceByGap.question: What is the correct monthly downtime allowance at 99.95% and at 99.99% over a 30-day month, and how did each month in the incident log perform against 99.95% (including whether a 22-minute month counts as a breach)?

evidence.claim: Schedule C clause C.1: the Provider shall make the Service available 99.95% of the time in each calendar month, measured over a 30-day month for SLA calculation purposes, excluding scheduled maintenance announced 72h in advance.
evidence.applicability: Sets the contractual target at 99.95%, not 99.99%. Directly relevant to C2 and C3.
evidence.limitations: This is an excerpt only. It does not define 'available' (e.g. partial degradation, error-rate thresholds) or how incidents are measured, and it says nothing on fees, termination, chronic breach or renewal.

evidence.claim: The 12-month incident log lists 7 incidents with customer-facing minutes: 2025-11 INC-311 bad deploy (config) 18; 2026-01 INC-327 bad deploy (schema migration) 38; 2026-02 INC-330 third-party payment API 9; 2026-04 INC-344 bad deploy (feature flag) 14; 2026-06 INC-358 single AZ outage (auto-failover worked) 3; 2026-08 INC-371 bad deploy (config) 22; 2026-09 INC-379 certificate expiry 11. The annotation reads: 'region-wide outages affecting us in last 12 months: 0'.
evidence.applicability: Primary data for the failure-cause mix (C1) and the monthly breach history (C2, C3).
evidence.limitations: Covers 12 months only. It is not checked against monitoring data, and it does not say whether minutes follow the contract's availability definition or maintenance exclusions. Months with no incident are not listed (presumably 0 minutes).

evidence.claim: VP Engineering's premise: the company should target 99.99%, which 'still gives us around 52 minutes of downtime a month', and region failure is the biggest risk. The project is proposed for next quarter at about $41k/month extra.
evidence.applicability: The premises under test (C2, C1).
evidence.limitations: This is a user-reported claim, and the evidence contradicts it (see E7, E1, E4).

evidence.claim: Over a 30-day month, 99.95% availability allows 21 minutes 36 seconds of downtime (4h22m48s per 365-day year), and 99.99% allows about 4.3 minutes per month. Average-month bases give 21.92 and 4.38 minutes. The ~52.6 minutes at 99.99% is the yearly allowance, not the monthly one.
evidence.applicability: Refutes the '52 minutes a month' premise (C2). The contract budget is 21.6 min per 30-day month.
evidence.limitations: Based on search-result snippets, not fetched pages. The canonical Google SRE availability table (https://sre.google/sre-book/availability-table/) appeared in results but could not be fetched (host not resolvable in this session). The 52.6 min/year figure is standard arithmetic (0.0001 x 525,600) and is not quoted from a snippet.

evidence.claim: Against the 21.6-minute monthly budget, two months exceeded the target: 2026-01 (38 min, roughly 99.912%) and 2026-08 (22 min, roughly 99.949%, which misses by about 0.4 min). All other months were within budget. A 'full 0.1%' shortfall below 99.95% (availability at or below 99.85%) needs at least 64.8 min of downtime in a 30-day month (21.6 + 43.2). No month came close, so on a truncating reading of C.2 no service credit was owed in the last 12 months.
evidence.applicability: Shows that SLA misses occurred but that credit exposure under C.2 has been $0 on this reading (C3). The 2026-08 miss is marginal.
evidence.limitations: My arithmetic and interpretation. If 'full 0.1%' is measured differently (e.g. from 100%), or partial credits are applied, the result changes. Assumes the log minutes equal contractually measured downtime and that no exclusions apply. The plan's '0.1% ~ 43 minutes' implies the first credit tier starts at 64.8 cumulative minutes, not 43.

evidence.claim: It is not known whether the incident log is complete or whether its customer-facing minutes match the contract's availability measurement (e.g. degraded-but-up states, maintenance exclusions, calendar vs 30-day month).
evidence.applicability: Affects whether the 2026-01 and 2026-08 months count as contractual breaches (C2, C3).
evidence.limitations: Requires comparing the log with monitoring data and the customer's SLA reports.

evidenceByGap.question: What is the realistic probability and typical duration of a full region outage at the provider and region in use, based on the provider's historical public incident record?

evidence.claim: AWS us-east-1 had a disruption on 19-20 October 2025, triggered by a latent race condition in DynamoDB's DNS management automation that left an empty DNS record for the regional endpoint. AWS's summary gives 11:48 PM PDT Oct 19 to 2:20 PM PDT Oct 20 (about 14.5 hours), with three distinct impact periods. Some secondary sources report about 15 hours.
evidence.applicability: Shows that regional outages do occur and can last many hours, which would exceed the monthly budget many times over (C6, G4). Relevant only if the company runs in us-east-1 or a similar region.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only. The aws.amazon.com fetch failed (host not resolvable in session). Duration figures differ by source: 14.5h, ~15h12m, and in the follow-up search 23:49 PDT Oct 19 to 15:01 PDT Oct 20, with another source saying the DNS issue itself was mitigated by 3:35 AM PDT. Customer impact varied by service, so not every workload was down for the full window. The trigger was regional, but its blast radius was not confined to us-east-1 workloads (see E21, E22).

evidence.claim: AWS us-east-1 had a disruption on 7 December 2021 that began at 7:30 AM PST and was triggered by an automated capacity-scaling activity on the internal network. Route 53 APIs were impaired until 2:30 PM PST (about 7 hours). Running EC2 instances were unaffected, but EC2 APIs errored. Secondary estimates run to more than 8 hours in total.
evidence.applicability: A second data point for multi-hour regional events at one major provider and region (G4, C6). Route 53 is a global service whose control-plane APIs were impaired by a us-east-1 event, which bears on DNS-based failover (see E28).
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only. Region-specific (us-east-1), and the provider and region in use here are unknown. The two incidents together do not give a rigorous annual probability.

evidence.claim: The provider and region the company uses are not stated, and no rigorous annual frequency of full-region outages could be established. The log reports 0 region-wide outages affecting the company in 12 months.
evidence.applicability: Limits how precisely expected regional-outage minutes can be compared with the observed deploy minutes (G4).
evidence.limitations: Public incident histories are anecdotal. Providers do not publish a base rate of region-wide failures.

evidence.claim: Premise: region failure is the biggest availability risk (VP Engineering).
evidence.applicability: The C1 premise under test.
evidence.limitations: The 12-month log contradicts it: 0 region-wide outages and 92/115 minutes from bad deploys.

evidence.claim: During the October 2025 us-east-1 event, AWS status updates (as quoted by secondary outlets) said that global services or features relying on US-EAST-1 endpoints, such as IAM updates and DynamoDB Global Tables, may also be experiencing issues. So the event was not confined to workloads hosted in us-east-1. Global control-plane functions anchored in that region were impaired.
evidence.applicability: D1/G4: a warm-standby or active-active second region at the same provider can still be impaired by a primary-region event if it depends on global control-plane functions such as IAM changes, global tables replication, or a us-east-1-homed control plane. It also means that during such an event, failover actions that need those control planes (e.g. IAM changes, provisioning) may themselves be degraded.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only. AWS's own wording is reached through secondary outlets; the AWS post-event summary could not be fetched (aws.amazon.com and docs.aws.amazon.com not resolvable in session). The snippets say IAM 'updates' (control-plane changes) were affected, not necessarily IAM authentication in other regions. The extent of impact on data planes in other regions is not established.

evidence.claim: Third-party analyses of the October 2025 AWS event argue that services outside us-east-1, including some with multi-region architecture, were affected because many dependencies route through us-east-1: 'geographic deployment and operational independence are not the same thing'.
evidence.applicability: D1: multi-region at one provider gives incomplete protection unless hidden global dependencies (IAM, STS, global tables, third-party SaaS hosted in us-east-1) are removed or tested.
evidence.limitations: Commentary, not AWS statements. The search summary did not attribute each quote to a specific URL, so the source mapping is approximate. Not fetched. A '142 services' figure in some blogs could not be verified.

evidence.claim: Google Cloud, 12 June 2025: a quota policy change with unintended blank fields was written to the regional Spanner tables used by Service Control (API authorization and quota) at about 10:45 AM PDT. The metadata replicated globally within seconds and crashed Service Control (secondary sources say a null pointer exception from a code path added 29 May without adequate error handling), impairing Google Cloud, Workspace and Security Operations services across many regions. The official status page lists the incident as 10:51 to 18:18 PDT. Google said existing streaming and IaaS resources were not directly affected by the primary failure, and committed to making Service Control fail open.
evidence.applicability: D1: a documented case where a globally replicated config/policy push in a shared control plane took down multiple regions at once. Multi-region deployment at the same provider would not have protected against it. It is the provider-scale analogue of the company's own config-deploy incidents (E3, E16).
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only; the official report was not fetched. Durations in secondary sources vary (about 3 hours to about 7 hours); 10:51-18:18 PDT is the official incident window, and many services recovered earlier. Null-pointer and 29 May details come from secondary write-ups.

evidence.claim: Microsoft Azure Front Door (AFD) and Azure CDN, 29 October 2025: customer configuration changes made across two different AFD control-plane build versions produced incompatible configuration metadata. Combined with a latent data-plane bug, this crashed AFD edge servers globally and impaired an internal DNS service. Customer impact ran from about 15:41 UTC on 29 Oct to 00:05 UTC on 30 Oct (some sources give a 15:45 start). A separate AFD incident on 9 October 2025 was also attributed to erroneous metadata propagating through the system.
evidence.applicability: D1: a second documented case where a global edge/DNS layer shared by all regions failed through config propagation. Any workload fronted by that global service was affected regardless of how many backend regions it used. Shows that a global traffic layer (CDN/front door/global DNS) is itself a single point of failure for multi-region designs.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets of secondary write-ups and status-page mirrors. The official Microsoft PIR (aka.ms/air/YKYN-BWZ) was not retrieved. The about 8.4 hour duration is my reading of the stated timestamps.

Candidates are progressive or canary deploys with automated rollback, safer schema migrations, config validation, certificate auto-renewal and monitoring, a third-party payment fallback, and warm-standby DR with a defined RTO.

evidence.claim: AWS DR guidance describes four strategies in increasing cost and complexity: backup and restore (lowest cost, longest RTO), pilot light (RTO/RPO in tens of minutes), warm standby (RTO/RPO in minutes) and multi-site active/active (RPO near zero, RTO potentially zero). Active/active is the most complex and should only be selected when business requirements necessitate it. In a worked example, AWS says pilot light or warm standby satisfies both the RTO and the cost criteria.
evidence.applicability: Supports warm standby or pilot light as cheaper hedges against region loss (C4, C6, G5).
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only; pages not fetched. RTO figures are generic design targets, not measured end-to-end times (see E28, E29). The 'pilot light or warm standby' conclusion comes from one worked example, not a general rule. No dollar costs given.

evidence.claim: A bad deploy, config push or expired certificate that is rolled out to both regions would take down both. Active-active therefore does not address the four bad-deploy incidents or the certificate expiry unless deploys are staged region-by-region with health gating. That staging (progressive rollout, automated rollback) can be done in a single region at much lower cost.
evidence.applicability: Explains why the proposed fix fits the observed failure modes poorly (C1). Provider-scale cases of the same failure class are in E23 and E24.
evidence.limitations: Reasoning from the log's cause categories, not empirical data on this system's deploy topology.

evidence.claim: No cost figures or downtime-reduction estimates were found for this company's targeted alternatives (canary/progressive deploys with automated rollback, schema-migration discipline, config validation, certificate auto-renewal and monitoring, payment-API fallback, warm standby).
evidence.applicability: Needed for the C4 TCO comparison.
evidence.limitations: Requires internal estimates from the platform team.

evidence.claim: Amazon Aurora Global Database (asynchronous storage-level cross-region replication): AWS documentation says that for managed failover, data loss depends on the cross-region replication lag at the time of failure. RPO is typically measured in seconds and RTO can be in the order of minutes. An AWS-authored design-patterns deck says secondary replicas typically lag the primary by under 1 second. An optional managed-RPO feature (Aurora PostgreSQL) monitors lag so that at least one secondary stays within a target RPO window.
evidence.applicability: D3/G6: typical RPO for managed asynchronous cross-region DB replication is seconds (sub-second typical lag), not zero. For a financial ledger, seconds of acknowledged-but-unreplicated writes may be lost on unplanned regional failover unless the business accepts that or uses synchronous replication (E31).
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only. The WebFetch of the docs page failed (docs.aws.amazon.com not resolvable in session). 'Under 1 second' is a typical figure from a conference deck, not a guarantee. Lag can spike under write load or network impairment. Figures apply to Aurora specifically; other databases (e.g. vanilla PostgreSQL or MySQL async replicas) will differ. The company's DB engine is unknown.

evidence.claim: An AWS Database Blog post on managed planned failovers states that Aurora Global Database does not provide a managed unplanned failover feature, which implies that unplanned regional failover required manual detach/promote steps.
evidence.applicability: D3: if current, manual promotion would add operator time to end-to-end RTO.
evidence.limitations: Single search snippet. The post appears to be dated and is likely superseded (see E27). Not fetched.

evidence.claim: A 2026 third-party guide describes unplanned Aurora Global Database failover via the failover-global-cluster command with --allow-data-loss, i.e. a managed unplanned failover that explicitly accepts losing unreplicated writes.
evidence.applicability: D3: confirms that unplanned failover on async replication is a data-loss-accepting operation, so RPO > 0 unless lag is zero at failure time.
evidence.limitations: Single third-party search snippet; not checked against the current AWS CLI reference (docs.aws.amazon.com not resolvable).

evidence.claim: An engineering blog's breakdown of a pilot light regional failover on AWS gives about 10-30 minutes end to end: detection via CloudWatch alarm or Route 53 health check about 1-2 minutes, Route 53 failover record update including TTL and propagation about 1-3 minutes, and scaling the recovery Auto Scaling group 5-15 minutes depending on AMI cache and warm-pool configuration. Warm standby avoids most of the scale-out step and is generally quoted at minutes of RTO. AWS architecture guidance notes that Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing controls act as highly available on/off switches for manually initiated failover.
evidence.applicability: D3/G5: even an optimistic automated pilot light failover (10-30 min) exceeds the 21.6-minute monthly budget, and a warm standby with human decision time will consume a large share of it. Neither prevents an SLA miss in a month with a regional event; both shorten it from hours (E10, E11) to minutes or tens of minutes.
evidence.limitations: The step breakdown comes from one blog (search snippet). The AWS sources corroborate only the qualitative points (warm standby RTO lower than pilot light; ARC for manual failover), not the minute figures. No official AWS end-to-end failover time was found. The figures exclude human decision/escalation time, DB promotion (E25) and client DNS caching beyond TTL, and they assume the control planes used for failover are healthy (cf. E11, E21).

evidence.claim: Other DR guides and study materials give much longer pilot light RTOs: 'tens of minutes to 1 hour', '30-60 minutes', and '1-4 hours'. Published example timings are described as design targets, not guarantees.
evidence.applicability: D3: realistic pilot light RTO ranges from tens of minutes to hours depending on automation, rehearsal and decision latency. Warm standby sits at the lower end.
evidence.limitations: Low-authority study-guide and vendor sources. The search summary did not map each figure to a specific URL, so per-figure attribution is uncertain. Snippets only.

evidence.claim: No authoritative figures were found for (a) MySQL semi-synchronous cross-region commit latency, (b) measured (as opposed to design-target) end-to-end warm standby failover times including human decision time, or (c) a vendor-published end-to-end regional failover time.
evidence.applicability: D3: limits how precisely the warm standby / pilot light alternative's SLA impact can be quantified.
evidence.limitations: Search budget exhausted. docs.aws.amazon.com and aws.amazon.com were not fetchable in this session.

evidence.claim: AWS DR guidance describes four strategies in increasing cost and complexity: backup and restore (lowest cost, longest RTO), pilot light (RTO/RPO in tens of minutes), warm standby (RTO/RPO in minutes) and multi-site active/active (RPO near zero, RTO potentially zero). Active/active is the most complex and should only be selected when business requirements necessitate it. In a worked example, AWS says pilot light or warm standby satisfies both the RTO and the cost criteria.
evidence.applicability: Supports warm standby or pilot light as cheaper hedges against region loss (C4, C6, G5).
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only; pages not fetched. RTO figures are generic design targets, not measured end-to-end times (see E28, E29). The 'pilot light or warm standby' conclusion comes from one worked example, not a general rule. No dollar costs given.

evidence.claim: Multi-leader active-active writes make conflicts unavoidable. Ledger-style invariants spanning multiple records are among the hardest cases, and two-site setups risk split-brain without a quorum or witness in a third location. Synchronous cross-region commits add round-trip latency to every write (one source says roughly 100-200 ms for cross-region Paxos). Common guidance: keep financial ledger writes strongly consistent, route each entity's writes to a home region, or default to active-passive.
evidence.applicability: Supports the C5 concern that multi-region writes on the ledger carry correctness and delivery risk, made worse because the consistency model is still TBD (E5).
evidence.limitations: Low-authority sources (blogs and interview-prep pages), seen only as search snippets. Latency figures are rough and depend on the region pair and the database. The 100-200 ms figure is not confirmed by an official vendor source (see E31).

evidence.claim: The estimate states 2 engineers x 2 quarters, and the ledger consistency model and RPO/RTO are TBD. That conflicts with delivering the project 'next quarter' as the request proposes.

evidence.claim: Amazon Aurora Global Database (asynchronous storage-level cross-region replication): AWS documentation says that for managed failover, data loss depends on the cross-region replication lag at the time of failure. RPO is typically measured in seconds and RTO can be in the order of minutes. An AWS-authored design-patterns deck says secondary replicas typically lag the primary by under 1 second. An optional managed-RPO feature (Aurora PostgreSQL) monitors lag so that at least one secondary stays within a target RPO window.
evidence.applicability: D3/G6: typical RPO for managed asynchronous cross-region DB replication is seconds (sub-second typical lag), not zero. For a financial ledger, seconds of acknowledged-but-unreplicated writes may be lost on unplanned regional failover unless the business accepts that or uses synchronous replication (E31).
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only. The WebFetch of the docs page failed (docs.aws.amazon.com not resolvable in session). 'Under 1 second' is a typical figure from a conference deck, not a guarantee. Lag can spike under write load or network impairment. Figures apply to Aurora specifically; other databases (e.g. vanilla PostgreSQL or MySQL async replicas) will differ. The company's DB engine is unknown.

evidence.claim: A 2026 third-party guide describes unplanned Aurora Global Database failover via the failover-global-cluster command with --allow-data-loss, i.e. a managed unplanned failover that explicitly accepts losing unreplicated writes.
evidence.applicability: D3: confirms that unplanned failover on async replication is a data-loss-accepting operation, so RPO > 0 unless lag is zero at failure time.
evidence.limitations: Single third-party search snippet; not checked against the current AWS CLI reference (docs.aws.amazon.com not resolvable).

evidence.claim: Google Cloud Spanner uses synchronous Paxos-based replication: voting replicas vote on every write, and a write commits once a majority agrees. In multi-region configurations every write needs a quorum across replicas in more than one region, so writes have higher latency than in single-region instances. Read-only replicas do not vote and do not add write latency. Google says RPO and RTO are 0 for a multi-region configuration when writes come from near the default leader region.
evidence.applicability: D3/G6: near-zero-RPO cross-region standby is achievable with synchronous quorum replication, at the cost of cross-region round-trip latency on every write. It typically needs three or more locations for quorum rather than two (consistent with E15's split-brain concern).
evidence.limitations: Snippets only. All sources are Google (different domains but the same vendor, so not fully independent). No specific millisecond figures retrieved from an official source. The 100-200 ms figure in E15 is from low-authority blogs, and actual cost depends on region-pair distance. Spanner-specific; adopting it would mean a database migration.

evidence.claim: An engineering post on cross-region single-leader replication (PostgreSQL) notes that synchronous cross-region acknowledgment puts the wide-area network directly into the commit path. A synchronous setting without selected standbys does not create cross-region durability, and acknowledgment alone does not guarantee zero loss of acknowledged writes if the primary site disappears before the standby catches up (e.g. remote_write vs applied semantics).
evidence.applicability: D3/G6: zero-RPO standby on a conventional RDBMS is possible with synchronous or semi-synchronous replication, but every commit then pays at least one cross-region round trip, and the guarantee depends on configuration details. This is a cheaper middle option than multi-writer active-active for the ledger.
evidence.limitations: Single third-party snippet. No latency numbers retrieved. MySQL semi-synchronous replication specifics were not found (see E32).

evidence.claim: No authoritative figures were found for (a) MySQL semi-synchronous cross-region commit latency, (b) measured (as opposed to design-target) end-to-end warm standby failover times including human decision time, or (c) a vendor-published end-to-end regional failover time.
evidence.applicability: D3: limits how precisely the warm standby / pilot light alternative's SLA impact can be quantified.

contradictions.aClaim: An engineering blog's breakdown of a pilot light regional failover on AWS gives about 10-30 minutes end to end: detection via CloudWatch alarm or Route 53 health check about 1-2 minutes, Route 53 failover record update including TTL and propagation about 1-3 minutes, and scaling the recovery Auto Scaling group 5-15 minutes depending on AMI cache and warm-pool configuration. Warm standby avoids most of the scale-out step and is generally quoted at minutes of RTO.
